title: The Maimed Hand: Lepanto, the Bagnos of Algiers, and the Book Begotten in a Prison
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Surgeon's Son on the Roads of Castile

stops.name: Alcala de Henares, the baptism at Santa Maria la Mayor
stops.date_confidence: attested: the baptismal entry of 9 October 1547 survives in the register of Santa Maria la Mayor. The birth date does not. The traditional 29 September is a back-formation from the name Miguel and the feast of Saint Michael, not a record of anything. The church itself was destroyed in 1936 in the Civil War; the tower, the Capilla del Oidor, and a 1905 reconstruction of the font are what stand.
stops.campa: The register records a child baptized Miguel, son of Rodrigo de Cervantes, surgeon-barber, and Leonor de Cortinas. No birth date is written anywhere. Later readers work backward from the name to the feast of Saint Michael on the twenty-ninth of September and set the birthday there, which is a guess wearing the clothes of a fact. The father sets bones and lets blood, a trade ranked below the university physicians, and claims an hidalgo standing that no paper confirms. Alcala is a university town; the child of the barber will never matriculate in it.
sources: Parish register of Santa Maria la Mayor, Alcala de Henares, cited in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography
es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iglesia_de_Santa_Maria_la_Mayor_(Alcala_de_Henares)
borges.journey.json, for the 1979 award of the Premio Cervantes in this city on 23 April
suggested_refs: The Capilla del Oidor and the reconstructed font at Santa Maria la Mayor, Alcala de Henares
Museo Casa Natal de Cervantes, Alcala de Henares

stops.name: Valladolid, the father in the debtors' prison
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, contested as to date. en.wikipedia dates the imprisonment October 1553 to April 1554; es.wikipedia dates the family's move to Valladolid to c. 1551 with the jailing following. The dossier's two lenses carried 1551 and 1553 against each other. The conflict is recorded, not settled.
stops.campa: Rodrigo de Cervantes is taken for debt and held from October into the following April. His goods are seized and his mother petitions to have them returned. The household of a boy of six becomes a household that owes money to people who can jail its head. What Miguel does or says that winter is not recorded, and he never writes about any of it afterwards. Notaries, bonds and seized furniture fill the books he makes fifty years later, and no line in them points back to this house.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The Chancilleria records of Valladolid concerning Rodrigo de Cervantes, 1553-1554

stops.name: Cordoba, the inheritance and the creditors
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. es.wikipedia gives 1556 for the father's move to Cordoba, to claim an inheritance and to put distance between himself and his Valladolid creditors. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The dossier's earlier range beginning 1553 is wrong at the front end.
stops.campa: Rodrigo moves south to Cordoba, where his own father Juan de Cervantes had lived, where there is an inheritance to claim, and where creditors from Valladolid cannot easily follow. The family stays years. Biographers put the boy in the Jesuit school here on the strength of a schoolroom scene in one of his late novellas and nothing else; no register carries his name. He is nine when he arrives. The Guadalquivir runs past a mosque made into a cathedral, and past a market where people are sold.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: El coloquio de los perros, the schoolroom passage read by biographers as Cordoban
The Jesuit college of Santa Catalina, Cordoba, whose registers do not name him

stops.name: Seville, the years with no record
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, not independently fetched this pass. The family is placed in Seville c. 1564-1566 by the standard biographies. Nothing documents Miguel here personally. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The family is thought to be in Seville about now, in the greatest port in the world, where the American silver comes ashore to be counted and stolen. Nothing documents Miguel in the city. The Jesuit college of Seville is proposed for him as Cordoba's was, on the same evidence, which is none at all. He is about seventeen. Valladolid, Cordoba, Seville, and next Madrid: a boyhood spent on the roads between them, in the train of a man outrunning what he owes.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies as relayed in the research dossier; not independently confirmed this pass
suggested_refs: The Casa de Contratacion and the Seville silver fleet, the city's economy in the 1560s

stops.name: Madrid, the school of Juan Lopez de Hoyos
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1569 printing, reconstructed for the years of study. The exact location of the estudio within Madrid is unknown, so the canonical Madrid pin is used. Month of the enrolment unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: In Madrid the humanist schoolmaster Juan Lopez de Hoyos keeps the city's estudio, and Cervantes is his pupil. When Queen Isabel de Valois dies in 1568, Lopez de Hoyos assembles a memorial volume and prints in it four poems by the young man. It is the first appearance of the name in print: age twenty-one, in a book about a dead queen. Where the school stood is not known, and no diploma or university matriculation is recorded for him here or anywhere else, then or later. What the record does hold is the schoolmaster's own phrase for him in the text: our dear and beloved pupil.
sources: Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography
Historia y relacion verdadera de la enfermedad, felicisimo transito y sumptuosas exequias funebres de la Serenissima Reyna de Espana Dona Isabel de Valoys, Madrid, 1569
suggested_refs: The 1569 memorial volume of Juan Lopez de Hoyos, first printing of Cervantes

stops.name: Madrid, the warrant for the right hand
stops.date_confidence: the document is attested and dated 15 September 1569; the identification is not certain. Most biographers take this fugitive Miguel de Cervantes to be the writer and read his sudden appearance in Italy that same year as flight. The name is not unique and no source settles it.
stops.campa: A royal order goes out for the arrest of one Miguel de Cervantes, who has wounded a man named Antonio de Sigura in a duel and fled. The sentence, if he is taken, is the public striking off of his right hand and ten years of banishment from the kingdom. Most of his biographers believe this fugitive is the writer. The identification cannot be proved and the name is not unique. What is certain is that he leaves Spain in 1569 and does not stand on Spanish ground again for eleven years, and that the hand the crown wanted was the right one.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The 1569 royal warrant naming Antonio de Sigura, Archivo General de Simancas

stops.name: Rome, the household of Giulio Acquaviva
stops.date_confidence: attested for the service, reconstructed for the month. Cervantes Project and en.wikipedia both place him in Acquaviva's household in Rome in 1569, before the prelate's elevation to cardinal in 1570.
stops.campa: He enters Rome as a chamber servant to Giulio Acquaviva, an Italian prelate who will be made cardinal within the year. Italy gives him the Ariosto and the Boccaccio he will still be arguing with in his sixties, and it gives him the working order of a great house seen from the servants' side of it. Behind him in Spain is a warrant for his hand. He has never sat in a university and never will. He is twenty-two, in another man's service, and out of reach of the courts that want him.
sources: Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The Roman household of Cardinal Giulio Acquaviva d'Aragona

stops.name: Naples, enlistment in the company of Diego de Urbina
stops.date_confidence: attested that he enlisted in 1570; the unit is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is stated in the campa rather than resolved. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He leaves the cardinal's household for a common soldier's pay and enlists at Naples in the company of Diego de Urbina, in the tercio of Miguel de Moncada, later called the tercio of the League. Naples is Spanish, the viceroyalty, the base of the Mediterranean fleet, and he will keep returning to it for five years between campaigns. English accounts put him instead in the tercio of Sicily under the Marques de Santa Cruz. The Spanish record names Urbina and Moncada. Nobody has reconciled the two readings.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes, giving Diego de Urbina and the tercio of Miguel de Moncada
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes, giving the Tercio of Sicily under the Marques de Santa Cruz
suggested_refs: Spanish muster rolls of the tercio de la Liga, 1570-1571

stops.name: Gulf of Patras, the seventh of October
stops.date_confidence: attested. The wounds, the galley Marquesa, and the refusal to stay below are given consistently in the biographical record and confirmed in substance by Cervantes himself in the 1613 preface to the Novelas ejemplares.
stops.campa: On the morning of the battle he is below decks with a fever and is told to stay there. He refuses, says he would rather die fighting for God and his king than keep himself safe, and is given twelve men at the skiff of the galley Marquesa. Something over two hundred ships of the Holy League meet the Ottoman fleet in the gulf. He takes three arquebus balls, two in the chest and one in the left hand, which never works again. He is twenty-four years old. Forty-two years later he is still calling it the highest occasion the past ages ever saw.
stops.quote: He lost his left hand by a musket-shot in the battle of Lepanto: and ugly as this wound may appear, he regards it as beautiful, having received it on the most memorable and sublime occasion which past times have ever seen, or future times can hope to equal
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Cervantes, preface to the Novelas ejemplares, 1613, trans. Walter K. Kelly. The Project Gutenberg transcription (#14420) reads 'over seen' for 'ever seen', an evident typographical error against the Spanish 'que vieron los pasados siglos'.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lepanto
The Exemplary Novels of Cervantes, trans. Walter K. Kelly, Project Gutenberg #14420
suggested_refs: The galley Marquesa in the order of battle of the Holy League fleet, 7 October 1571

stops.name: Messina, six months in the hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested for the hospitalization and the pay increase; the month of admission is inferred from the fleet's return to Messina after the battle.
stops.campa: The fleet brings its wounded back to Messina and he is put in the hospital there, where he stays into the spring. The hand does not recover. It is not cut off, whatever the nickname will say: it hangs at his side, dead, for forty-five more years. He is granted extra pay for the wounds, three escudos above the ordinary, and a certificate of his conduct at Lepanto, signed by his commanders. He will spend the rest of his life presenting that certificate to officials who put it down again.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lepanto, for the Holy League fleet's sailing from and return to Messina
suggested_refs: The Lepanto conduct certificates of Don Juan of Austria and the Duke of Sessa, carried by Cervantes in 1575

stops.name: Navarino, the war that does not end at Lepanto
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The post-Lepanto Greek operations at Corfu, Navarino, and Modon are named in the standard biographies and in the dossier chronology, none of it independently fetched this pass. Month approximate, set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is back at sea within months, in Lope de Figueroa's command, and the fleet works the Greek coast: Corfu, Navarino, Modon. At Navarino the Christian fleet has the Ottoman ships shut in the bay and does not close, and Ulug Ali gets out. Nothing happens that anyone writes a poem about. This is the ordinary matter of the Mediterranean war, wind and rowing and a coast that will not be taken, and it is what he does for four years after the famous morning. He is a soldier of the fleet from 1570 to 1575.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies as relayed in the research dossier; not independently confirmed this pass
suggested_refs: The 1572 Holy League campaign on the Peloponnesian coast under Lope de Figueroa

stops.name: La Goleta, the taking of Tunis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to his personal presence, attested as to the expedition. The dossier's range 1573-1574 was wrong: the 1574 events at La Goleta are the Ottoman recapture, which he was not part of. es.wikipedia places him in 1574-1575 in Sicily, Sardinia, Genoa, Lombardy, and Naples.
stops.campa: Don Juan of Austria takes Tunis and the fortress of La Goleta on the African shore, and Cervantes is in the expedition. The Spanish hold it under a year. In 1574 the Ottomans come back and take it for good, and he is not there for that, being by then in Sicily and Sardinia and Genoa and Lombardy with the tercios. Forty years later he will put the fall of La Goleta into Don Quixote, in the mouth of a captive soldier telling his life to strangers at an inn in La Mancha. This is the first African ground he stands on. He is twenty-six years old.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes, giving the 1573 occupation of Tunis and La Goulette
es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The Captive's Tale, Don Quixote Part 1 chapters XXXIX-XLI, which narrates the loss of La Goleta in 1574

segments.name: Algiers: Five Years and Four Attempts

stops.name: Off Palamos, the galley El Sol
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia gives the capture as approaching Barcelona on 26 September 1575. The precise position off the Catalan coast is approximate; Palamos is the conventional landfall named in the biographies.
stops.campa: He sails from Naples for Spain with his brother Rodrigo aboard the galley El Sol, carrying letters of recommendation from Don Juan of Austria and the Duke of Sessa, addressed to the king, asking that this soldier be given a company of his own. Three galiots under the corsair Arnaut Mami take the ship near the Catalan coast, within sight of the country he has not seen in six years. The captors read the letters and conclude they have caught somebody important. The recommendations that were to make his career set his ransom at five hundred escudos.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The letters of Don Juan of Austria and the Duke of Sessa, lost with the capture of El Sol

stops.name: Algiers, the letters that set the price
stops.date_confidence: attested for the captivity and the ransom economy; the assignment to Dali Mami and the month of arrival are reconstruction from the standard biographies and the 1580 depositions.
stops.campa: Algiers holds something like twenty-five thousand Christian captives and runs an economy on their ransom, and Cervantes is entered into it as a valuable man. He is assigned to the Greek renegade Dali Mami, who has read the letters. He is not sent to the oar; a man worth five hundred escudos is kept whole and kept in the city. That is what makes everything that follows possible, because a captive who can walk about Algiers can plan. Forty years on he will write that captivity is the greatest evil that can fall to the lot of man.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers
suggested_refs: Los banos de Argel and El trato de Argel, Cervantes's own plays of the captivity
Informacion de Argel, the twelve depositions of 1580

stops.name: Near Oran, the guide who abandons them
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The first escape attempt is known only from the depositions gathered for the Informacion de Argel in 1580, which were not read in the original or in a scholarly edition this pass. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The first attempt. He and a few others walk out of Algiers meaning to reach the Spanish presidio at Oran, better than two hundred miles west along the coast, with a Moorish guide hired to take them there. The guide leaves them on the road. They have no water, no language, and no way forward, and they turn back to Algiers and to whatever is waiting. Everything known about this comes from depositions taken in 1580 at Cervantes's own request; there is no other source, and every escape in this segment rests on the word of the men who tried it with him.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies reporting the Informacion de Argel, 1580; not independently fetched this pass
suggested_refs: Informacion de Argel, 1580, the sworn depositions of twelve fellow captives

stops.name: Coastal cave east of Algiers, El Dorador
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The cave's precise place on the coast is not fixed in any record and the coordinates are approximate. Month set to order the segment. Source is the 1580 depositions as relayed by the standard biographies.
stops.campa: Second attempt. His brother Rodrigo, ransomed and home, arranges a ship to come for them, and Cervantes hides fifteen men in a cave outside the city and keeps them alive there for months, fed by a gardener the captives call El Saylan. The vessel arrives, is driven off, comes back. Then the go-between they call El Dorador sells the whole plan to Hasan Pasha. Cervantes tells the pasha the plan was his and names nobody else. The men are brought up out of the rock after months inside it and marched back into the city.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies reporting the Informacion de Argel, 1580; not independently fetched this pass
suggested_refs: Informacion de Argel, 1580, on the cave, the gardener, and the betrayal by El Dorador

stops.name: Algiers, Hasan Pasha's bagno
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the location within Algiers, which is approximated, and as to the months. The third attempt of 1578, a letter carried overland to Oran whose messenger was impaled, is folded into this stop and rests on the same depositions.
stops.campa: He is moved into the governor's own bath-prison and kept under guard. Hasan Pasha, the Venetian renegade who rules Algiers, does not kill him. He has him bound and threatened and questioned. In 1578 he has the messenger Cervantes sent overland to Oran impaled, and sentences Cervantes himself to two thousand blows, and then does not have them given. The captives' depositions say the pasha reckoned his city and his captives safe as long as he had the maimed Spaniard under lock. Why he spared the man four times over, no source says.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
Standard Cervantes biographies reporting the Informacion de Argel, 1580
suggested_refs: The bagno of Hasan Pasha, setting of Cervantes's play Los banos de Argel

stops.name: Algiers, the sixty men of Onofre Exarque
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Fourth attempt, 1579, from the 1580 depositions as relayed in the standard biographies; not independently fetched this pass. Month approximate.
stops.campa: The fourth attempt, and the largest. A Valencian merchant named Onofre Exarque puts up the money for a frigate to carry sixty captives out at once, and a renegade called Cabrera is to sail it. A Dominican, Juan Blanco de Paz, informs on the plan to the pasha. Cervantes is brought before Hasan Pasha with a rope around his neck and says again that the plan was his alone, and names nobody. He is not executed. Exarque, terrified of what will be extracted from him next, offers to pay the whole ransom outright to get the man out of the country.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies reporting the Informacion de Argel, 1580; not independently fetched this pass
suggested_refs: Informacion de Argel, 1580, taken in part to answer Juan Blanco de Paz's counter-accusations

stops.name: Algiers, five hundred gold escudos
stops.date_confidence: attested. The ransom of 500 gold escudos, completed 19 September 1580 by Fray Juan Gil, is confirmed in es.wikipedia and the standard chronologies. The detail that Hasan Pasha's galleys were already loading for Constantinople is traditional.
stops.campa: The Trinitarian friars Juan Gil and Anton de la Bella collect the ransom: five hundred gold escudos, made up out of his mother's savings, his sister Andrea's dowry money, alms begged across Spain, and merchants' loans raised on the spot in Algiers. Hasan Pasha has his galleys loading for Constantinople and Cervantes is aboard one of them, in irons, when the money is counted. He is thirty-three and has been a slave for five years. Before he sails he asks the friars to take sworn depositions from the other captives about how he conducted himself.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The Trinitarian redemption accounts of Fray Juan Gil, Algiers, September 1580

stops.name: Denia, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested. es.wikipedia gives 24 October 1580 for the arrival at Denia, then Valencia, then Madrid by November or December. The dossier's 27 October is three days out and was corrected. Coordinates are the canonical Denia pin already in use in the corpus.
stops.campa: He comes ashore at Denia on the Valencian coast on the twenty-fourth of October, a free man standing in Spain for the first time since 1569. From here he goes up to Valencia, then inland, and reaches Madrid before the year is out. The port is a small one and nobody records the arrival except himself. He is thirty-three, and what he carries up the road is a certificate from Lepanto and a sheaf of sworn testimony taken in Algiers. He has no money and no post.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denia
suggested_refs: The Trinitarian redemption of 1580 and its return route through Valencia

stops.name: Madrid, the Informacion de Argel
stops.date_confidence: attested that he returned to Madrid late in 1580 and that the depositions were filed; the month is approximate. Cervantes Project has him returned to his family in Madrid.
stops.campa: He files the depositions in Madrid: twelve witnesses, sworn before a notary in Algiers, describing five years of a man who planned four escapes, took the blame each time, and named no one. It is a legal instrument built to be presented at court, and it remains the fullest documentary record of his life that exists anywhere. He presents it. The crown reads it, or does not, and gives him a few small errands, one of them back to Africa, to Oran. He is not made a captain. Years later he asks for a post in the Indies and is told to look for something closer to home.
sources: Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: Informacion de Argel, 1580, Archivo General de Indias
Cervantes's 1590 petition for a post in the Indies, and the endorsement refusing it

stops.name: Lisbon, the court of the new crown
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. His presence at Lisbon in 1581, where Philip II's court was administering the newly acquired Portuguese crown, is standard in the biographies and was not independently fetched this pass. Month approximate.
stops.campa: Philip II has taken Portugal and is holding court at Lisbon, and the whole apparatus of Spanish patronage moves there for a season with Cervantes among it. He is sent on an errand to Oran, in the same Africa he was a slave in, and paid a little for the trip. Nothing else comes of the journey. The court holds thousands of war records and a limited number of pensions, and the kingdom has just doubled in size without making room for him. He goes on presenting his papers for another four years.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies as relayed in the research dossier; not independently confirmed this pass
suggested_refs: The Iberian Union of 1580 and the Lisbon court of Philip II

stops.name: Madrid, Isabel at Santos Justo y Pastor
stops.date_confidence: attested. The baptismal entry of 9 April 1584 at Santos Justo y Pastor was located by Emilio Maganto Pavon and supersedes the older guesswork. The dossier's 'November 1584' and its 'Ana Franca de Rojas' are both wrong: the birth is March 1584, the mother is Ana de Villafranca y Rojas. The item is raised from reconstruction to attested.
stops.campa: A daughter is baptized in the parish of Santos Justo y Pastor: Isabel, born the month before to Ana de Villafranca y Rojas, the wife of a tavernkeeper named Alonso Rodriguez. She is Cervantes's only child. He acknowledges her, takes her into the household after her mother dies, and quarrels with her over money and property for years; she signs herself Isabel de Saavedra, taking the name he himself preferred. The baptismal entry was found in the twentieth century by Emilio Maganto Pavon and settles what had been three centuries of speculation.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabel_de_Saavedra
Emilio Maganto Pavon's location of the baptismal record, cited there
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Santos Justo y Pastor, Madrid, 9 April 1584

stops.name: Esquivias, the marriage to Catalina
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage at Esquivias in December 1584; the day is the conventional date given in the biographies. The itemized dowry is reconstruction from the standard biographies, not independently fetched this pass.
stops.campa: Eight months after the birth in Madrid he marries, in the wine town of Esquivias in the Toledo country, Catalina de Salazar y Palacios. He is thirty-seven and she is about nineteen. Her dowry is set down item by item: vines, an orchard, some furniture, four beehives, forty-five hens and a rooster. There are no children of the marriage. Within three years he will be in Andalusia on the king's business, and of the thirty-one years the marriage lasts he will spend the better part of fifteen away from her.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquivias
suggested_refs: The marriage contract and dowry inventory of Catalina de Salazar, Esquivias, 1584

stops.name: Alcala de Henares, La Galatea
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication in 1585 at Alcala de Henares; the month is not carried in the dossier and defaults to January. The death of his father Rodrigo in the same year is attested.
stops.campa: His first book is printed in the town he was baptized in: La Galatea, a pastoral romance of shepherds who are courtiers in disguise, dedicated to Ascanio Colonna. It sells poorly. He promises a second part on its last page, promises it again in the prologue to Don Quixote twenty years later, promises it once more on his deathbed at sixty-eight, and never writes a line of it. His father Rodrigo dies the same year, still a surgeon-barber, still short of money.
sources: Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: Primera parte de La Galatea, Alcala de Henares, Juan Gracian, 1585

stops.name: Seville, commissioner of provisions
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment in 1587 and the Andalusian provisioning work under Antonio de Guevara; the details of the circuit are reconstruction from the standard administrative record as relayed in the dossier. Month defaults to January.
stops.campa: He takes a job. Antonio de Guevara is assembling supplies in Andalusia for the fleet the king is building against England, and Cervantes is made a commissioner: he rides from town to town requisitioning wheat, barley, and oil at prices the crown sets, against receipts the crown is slow to honour. He is competent at it and it makes him hated in every place he enters. The Armada sails in 1588 and is destroyed. The requisitioning does not stop, because there is always another fleet, and he keeps riding the same roads for ten years.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
Standard Cervantes biographies as relayed in the research dossier
suggested_refs: The provisioning accounts of Antonio de Guevara, Archivo General de Simancas

stops.name: Ecija, the granaries and the excommunications
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The excommunications for seizing church grain are standard in the biographical literature and were not independently confirmed this pass. Ecija is one town of a circuit; the date is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: At Ecija he takes grain belonging to the cathedral chapter and is excommunicated for it. It happens more than once in these years and he treats it as a hazard of the trade. The town councils petition against him and the clergy curse him from the altar. The wheat leaves in the carts anyway. The inns and muleteers and notaries of the later novel are all on these roads, and he is not writing yet: he is riding from one dusty Andalusian town to the next with an escort and a warrant, counting sacks and signing for them.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies as relayed in the research dossier; not independently confirmed this pass
suggested_refs: Municipal petitions of the Andalusian towns against the royal commissioners, 1587-1593

stops.name: Castro del Rio, the first prison
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was briefly jailed at Castro del Rio in 1592 by order of the corregidor of Ecija; the month is approximate. The file holds an accusation and no conviction.
stops.campa: The corregidor of Ecija has him arrested and jailed at Castro del Rio over a quantity of wheat he is said to have sold without authorization. He is out within days. There is an accusation in the file and there is no conviction. It is the smaller of the two prisons in his life, and the shape is the same in both: he works for the crown, the crown does not pay him, and the crown locks him up over the paperwork. He is forty-five years old. Lepanto was twenty-one years ago.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
suggested_refs: The order of the corregidor of Ecija committing Cervantes to Castro del Rio, 1592

stops.name: Granada, the arrears of the kingdom
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1594 commission to collect tax arrears in the kingdom of Granada and the deposit with the banker Simon Freire de Lima are drawn from general biographical consensus and were not confirmed against a fetched documentary source. Month defaults to January.
stops.campa: A new commission sends him into the kingdom of Granada to collect tax arrears, some millions of maravedis owed by towns with no intention of paying. He collects what he can and deposits it in Seville with a banker named Simon Freire de Lima, for transfer to the treasury in Madrid. That is the ordinary way to move money across Spain and there is nothing irregular in it. Freire's bank then fails, and the crown, which is owed the sum, goes looking for the official whose name is on the receipt.
sources: Standard Cervantes biographies as relayed in the research dossier; not independently confirmed this pass
suggested_refs: The Granada tax-arrears commission of 1594 and the failure of Simon Freire de Lima's bank

stops.name: Seville, the royal jail
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Cervantes Project that he was jailed in Seville in 1597; the order of Judge Gaspar de Vallejo and the connection to Freire's failure are widely reported but were not confirmed against a fetched archival source this pass. Month approximate. No conviction for embezzlement is documented.
stops.campa: Judge Gaspar de Vallejo orders him held in the royal prison of Seville while the accounts are gone through. He is inside for some months. It is not a conviction for theft; it is a debt the crown fastens to the man who handled the money. Eight years later the prologue to Don Quixote says the book was begotten in a prison, where every discomfort has its seat and every dismal sound its habitation, and readers have taken that to mean this building ever since, without a single line of evidence that it does.
stops.quote: Idle reader: thou mayest believe me without any oath that I would this book, as it is the child of my brain, were the fairest, gayest, and cleverest that could be imagined.
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Cervantes, Author's Preface to Don Quixote Part 1, 1605, trans. John Ormsby (1885)
sources: Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography
Don Quixote Part 1, Author's Preface, trans. John Ormsby, via Wikisource

stops.name: Valladolid, the house on the Calle del Rastro
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the address, which is documented by the 1605 homicide proceeding; the year of arrival is approximate and the month defaults to January. The dossier's coordinates and its street name 'Rastro de los Carneros' were both wrong and were replaced with the documented values from es.wikipedia.
stops.campa: The court moves to Valladolid and Cervantes moves with it, into a rented upper floor on the Calle del Rastro beside the slaughterhouse, with his wife, his two sisters, his niece, and his daughter Isabel. The neighbours call the household las Cervantas and mean by it what they mean. He is fifty-six years old, has published one pastoral romance nobody read, and is finishing a long comic book about a country gentleman who has read too many other books. The house still stands. What fixes the address in the record is a murder investigation.

stops.name: Madrid, Juan de la Cuesta sets the first line
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication in Madrid in January 1605 by Juan de la Cuesta for the bookseller Francisco de Robles, and for the immediate reprints and piracies.
stops.campa: The printer Juan de la Cuesta, in the Calle de Atocha, brings out El ingenioso hidalgo don Quixote de la Mancha for the bookseller Francisco de Robles: badly set, full of errors, and by summer pirated in Lisbon and Valencia and read aloud in the street, with Quixote and Sancho got up as figures in carnival processions. Cervantes sold the rights outright and makes almost nothing. Three centuries later Jorge Luis Borges, who first read this book in English as a boy in his father's library, will publish a story in which a Frenchman rewrites it word for word and produces something richer.
stops.quote: In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind, there lived not long since one of those gentlemen that keep a lance in the lance-rack, an old buckler, a lean hack, and a greyhound for coursing.
stops.quote_source: Don Quixote Part 1, Chapter I, trans. John Ormsby (1885)

stops.name: Valladolid, the night Gaspar de Ezpeleta is cut down
stops.date_confidence: attested. The wounding on the night of 27 June 1605 and the subsequent proceeding are documented. Ezpeleta was carried into an adjoining dwelling in the same building, not into the Cervantes lodging, and died two days later; the dossier had him dying inside their rooms on the 27th and that is corrected here.
stops.campa: On the night of the twenty-seventh of June a knight of Santiago named Gaspar de Ezpeleta is run through in the street outside the building and is carried in to a neighbour's rooms on the same stair, where he dies two days later. The judge Cristobal de Villarroel takes the whole house into custody: Cervantes, his wife, his sisters, his daughter, the widows and seamstresses on the upper floors. The women's visitors are gone into at length and in public. Nothing is found against anyone and all are released. Nobody is ever tried for the killing.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Cervantes_(Valladolid)

stops.name: Madrid, the court comes back
stops.date_confidence: attested that the household returned to Madrid with the court in 1606-1607; Cervantes Project gives 1607 for the settling. The street list is reconstruction from the standard biographies. The Franciscan Third Order affiliation of 1613 is reported widely and was not independently confirmed this pass.
stops.campa: Philip III returns the court to Madrid and the household follows it, into rented rooms in the quarter of the writers: Calle de la Magdalena, Calle del Leon, Calle de las Huertas, Calle de Francos. Lope de Vega lives a few streets off and does not like him. Cervantes is fifty-nine, famous, and poor. He joins a devotional confraternity and, in 1613, the Franciscan Third Order as a lay member, which is how a Madrid man of his age arranges his burial. He has ten years to live and two books published.
sources: Cervantes Project, Texas A&M University, biography

stops.name: Madrid, the twelve novellas and the face nobody painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication of the Novelas ejemplares in 1613 and for the self-portrait in its preface. The absence of any authenticated lifetime likeness is a negative finding, reported as art-historical consensus and not disprovable from any source reached this pass.
stops.campa: He publishes the Novelas ejemplares, twelve short fictions, and claims in the preface to be the first who ever wrote the novella in Castilian instead of translating it out of the Italian. The preface opens by apologizing that there is no engraved portrait at the front of the book, and then supplies one in words. No authenticated likeness of Cervantes made in his lifetime exists. The famous ruff-collared painting rests on a line in this same preface saying that Juan de Jauregui could have painted him, and on inscriptions added later by other hands.
stops.quote: This person whom you see here, with an oval visage, chestnut hair, smooth open forehead, lively eyes, a hooked but well-proportioned nose... silvery beard that twenty years ago was golden, large moustaches, a small mouth, teeth not much to speak of
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Cervantes, preface to the Novelas ejemplares, 1613, trans. Walter K. Kelly, Project Gutenberg #14420
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
The Exemplary Novels of Cervantes, trans. Walter K. Kelly, Project Gutenberg #14420

stops.name: Madrid, the false Quixote out of Tarragona
stops.date_confidence: attested that the unauthorized continuation was published at Tarragona in 1614 under the name Alonso Fernandez de Avellaneda, whose identity remains unresolved. The month of Cervantes's learning of it is approximate. The stop is placed in Madrid, where he was, and not at Tarragona, where he never went.
stops.campa: A second part of Don Quixote appears at Tarragona under the name Alonso Fernandez de Avellaneda, whom nobody has ever identified, and whose preface calls Cervantes old, one-handed, envious, and without friends. Cervantes is sixty-seven and has been at work on his own second part for years. He answers in his own preface, not by denying the age or the hand but by insisting on where the hand was lost. Then he takes the false book into the true one, and lets his own characters read it and argue with it.
stops.quote: If my wounds have no beauty to the beholder's eye, they are, at least, honourable in the estimation of those who know where they were received
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Cervantes, Author's Preface to Don Quixote Part 2, 1615, trans. John Ormsby (1885)
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes

stops.name: Madrid, the second part, and eight plays never staged
stops.date_confidence: attested for all three books: Viaje del Parnaso 1614, Ocho comedias y ocho entremeses nuevos 1615, and the authentic Segunda parte 1615. The stop is dated to the Segunda parte and gathers the other two, since they belong to the same two years of work.
stops.campa: In the last two years of his life he publishes the Viaje del Parnaso, a mock-heroic survey of the poets of Spain; the Ocho comedias y ocho entremeses nuevos, whose title page states plainly that not one of them has ever been performed; and the Segunda parte del ingenioso caballero don Quixote de la Mancha, in which the knight rides to Barcelona instead of Zaragoza for the express reason that the false book sent him to Zaragoza. In Buenos Aires three centuries on, Alberto Gerchunoff will spend a working life writing about these two volumes.
stops.quote: Freedom, Sancho, is one of the most precious gifts that heaven has bestowed upon men; no treasures that the earth holds buried or the sea conceals can compare with it; for freedom, as for honour, life may and should be ventured; and on the other hand, captivity is the greatest evil that can fall to the lot of man.
stops.quote_source: Don Quixote Part 2, Chapter LVIII, trans. John Ormsby (1885)
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes
Don Quixote Part 2, Chapter LVIII, trans. John Ormsby, via Wikisource

stops.name: Madrid, the foot in the stirrup
stops.date_confidence: attested. Death on 22 April 1616. Hidropesia, dropsy, is a description of fluid retention and not a diagnosis; retrospective guesses at diabetes, liver, cardiac, or renal disease cannot be proven and are not asserted here. Extreme unction on the eighteenth, the Persiles dedication dated the nineteenth.
stops.campa: He is ill with what the century calls hidropesia, dropsy, meaning swelling and a thirst that cannot be answered, and nobody now can say what the disease was. On the eighteenth of April he receives extreme unction. On the nineteenth he sits up and writes the dedication of Persiles to the Count of Lemos, quoting an old song about a man with one foot already in the stirrup, and takes his leave of wit and of his friends. He dies on the twenty-second, aged sixty-eight, in the rented house on the corner of the Calle del Leon.
stops.quote: With my foot in the stirrup already, And the terrors of death before my eyes, I write, noble Marquis, to thee.
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Cervantes, dedication of Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda to the Count of Lemos, 19 April 1616, trans. Louisa Dorothea Stanley, Project Gutenberg #61561. Cervantes notes there that he is quoting an old couplet, not coining the line.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes

stops.name: Madrid, buried in the Franciscan habit at the Trinitarias
stops.date_confidence: attested. Burial on 23 April 1616 at the Convento de las Trinitarias Descalzas. Coordinates are the documented ones from es.wikipedia; the dossier's afterlife lens carried a point some 290 m off on four separate items and it is corrected throughout. The burial date was for centuries printed as the death date.
stops.campa: He is carried the short distance to the convent of the Discalced Trinitarians on the Calle de Cantarranas, face uncovered as the Third Order requires, in a Franciscan habit, and buried inside. He had asked for it. The Trinitarians are the order whose friars bought him out of Algiers thirty-six years earlier for five hundred gold escudos, and this is what he had to give them back. The burial entry survives and the grave does not. For centuries the date on that entry, the twenty-third, was printed as the date of his death.
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convento_de_las_Trinitarias_Descalzas

stops.name: Madrid, the widow prints Persiles
stops.date_confidence: attested for the posthumous publication of Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda in January 1617, arranged by Catalina de Salazar. Her burial at the same convent is attested.
stops.campa: Catalina de Salazar, nineteen when she married him and his wife for thirty-one years, sees Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda through the press. It is a Byzantine romance of pilgrims crossing the frozen north toward Rome, written by a man who never travelled further north than Barcelona. He thought it the best thing he had done. It is the one nobody reads. The dedication he wrote three days before dying is still bound at the front of it. She dies in 1626 and is buried at the same Trinitarian convent.
stops.quote: Adieu to gaiety, adieu to wit, adieu, my pleasant friends, for I am dying, yet hoping to see you all again happy in another world.
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Cervantes, dedication of Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda to the Count of Lemos, 19 April 1616, trans. Louisa Dorothea Stanley, Project Gutenberg #61561

stops.name: Madrid, the crypt rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: attested that the convent church was rebuilt in the later seventeenth century and that the burials in the old crypt were disturbed, moved, and commingled. 1673 is the year conventionally given for the works; the month is not recorded and defaults to January.
stops.campa: The convent church is pulled about and rebuilt, and the burials in the old crypt are dug up, moved, and put back in mixed together. No marker had ever been set over him and none is set now. From this point there is no grave of Cervantes at all, only a building that contains him along with everyone else who was buried in it, and for the next three hundred years a country that raises his statue in every city has nothing it can point to and say he is under there. The date usually given for the works is 1673.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes

stops.name: Madrid, the board marked M.C.
stops.date_confidence: attested. The search ran 2011 to 2015 under the historian Fernando de Prado with the forensic anthropologist Francisco Etxeberria; the crypt and the coffin fragment marked M.C. were located in January 2015. TIME reported DNA testing as pending.
stops.campa: A search begun in 2011 by the historian Fernando de Prado, with the forensic anthropologist Francisco Etxeberria, goes through the convent floor with ground-penetrating radar and infrared and finds a crypt, and in the crypt a fragment of coffin board with the letters M.C. set into it in tacks. Around it lie the commingled bones of at least fifteen people, adults and children, in the right place, of the right date. No single skeleton is separated out. No DNA comparison is made, there being nothing on earth to compare it against.
sources: TIME, 'Spain Searches for Cervantes' Tomb', time.com/3747402

stops.name: Madrid, fifteen people reinterred as one
stops.date_confidence: attested for the June 2015 reinterment. The identification is contested: English Wikipedia reported the remains as confirmed as Cervantes's, partly by reference to the Lepanto wounds, which is a stronger claim than the excavators themselves made. TIME's contemporaneous reporting treated the identification as historical and circumstantial.
stops.campa: In June the remains are put back under the floor of the same church in an ossuary, with a ceremony, the mayor, and a marble slab, four hundred years after the burial. The press reports that the bones of Cervantes have been found and identified. What was found is a heap of bones that certainly contains him and cannot be sorted, which is the truer sentence and the one the excavators actually said. He goes back into the floor with the other fourteen, unnamed and unseparated, which is more or less the condition he was buried in the first time.
sources: TIME, 'Spain Searches for Cervantes' Tomb', time.com/3747402
